description.value: An fMRI study examined how low and high working-memory load affected behavioral and neural responses to control, neutral, and smoking-related distractors in daily cigarette smokers.

spans.text: The goal of the current study was to address this important knowledge gap by characterizing the effect of cognitive load on behavioral and neural responses to smoking cues.

value: we predicted that performance of daily smokers (n=17) would be most impaired when high load was paired with smoking distractors.
Additionally, we predicted that smoking distractors would be associated with increased activation in frontal regions associated with selective attention in the presence of distracting stimuli.

spans.text: We expected that smoking cue distractors would interfere with limited working memory resources and task performance would be most impaired on high load trials paired with smoking-related stimuli.

The GLM contained a total of nine task-related regressors, each modeled using a box-car function convolved with a standard two-gamma hemodynamic response function: regressors for the encoding phase of low load (3-second duration) and high load (6-second duration) trials; six regressors for the delay phase of trials (control, neutral cue, and smoking cue conditions, each under low and high load; 10-second duration); and a regressor for the memory probe/response phase of trials (3-second duration).
